information_for_contributors: Combined grammar for JASS: a token layer that follows the language's lexing rules, plus a line-anchored layer for declarations and statements, since JASS requires every declaration and statement to appear on its own line.

Correctness depends on rule ORDER and TextMate's leftmost-match-wins scanning: the engine picks the match that starts earliest in the line and breaks same-offset ties by position in the patterns array. Three invariants follow:

1. Keyword and number rules have NO leading word boundary. A numeric literal ends at the first character outside its digit set, so '0then' is '0' + keyword 'then' and '0xFthen' is '0xF' + 'then'. A leading \b would break those.

2. #identifier is load-bearing, not cosmetic. It always matches a full [A-Za-z_][0-9A-Za-z_]* run starting at its leftmost character, which is what keeps keyword/number rules from matching in the middle of one ('myif' or 'abc0then' stay single identifiers). It must stay after #keywords and #function-call, and before #illegal.

3. Rules sharing a start character are ordered longest-token-first because the engine does NOT prefer the longest match: '==' before '=', hex before decimal, real before octal, bad-octal (contains 8/9) before octal, 'elseif' before 'else'.

Name/type slots in declarations use capture sub-patterns that try #keywords first and fall back to the slot's own scope. This replaces per-rule keyword-exclusion lookaheads for colouring: when a keyword lands in a name slot it simply keeps its keyword colour, so malformed lines degrade to plain token highlighting instead of mis-scoping. The two guards that do exist - the function name slot and the parameter name slot refusing 'takes'/'returns' - are structural, not cosmetic: they keep those keywords unconsumed so the meta.function clause regions can open and close at them.

The function signature follows the meta.function scope convention: meta.function (the head), meta.function.parameters (the takes-clause) and meta.function.return-type (the returns-clause) alternate instead of stacking. That is why the signature wrapper region has no name of its own - a named wrapper would stack over every clause - and why the clause regions close by lookahead before 'returns', a trailing comment, or the end of the line.

Scope naming follows https://www.sublimetext.com/docs/scope_naming.html. The decisions easiest to accidentally undo: entity.name.* appears ONLY at definition sites - entity.name.function in a function declaration's name slot, entity.name.type in a type declaration's - while invocations and 'function Foo' references are variable.function, type USAGES are support.type (outside the primitives, every type a script can name is declared by common.j, so a usage is a library reference), and the extends slot is entity.other.inherited-class. Declaration keywords carry keyword.declaration.* alongside storage.type.* for backwards compatibility, word operators carry keyword.operator.word alongside keyword.operator.logical, strings carry meta.string, and constant globals are variable.other.constant. Grammar-specific qualifiers sit only after a sanctioned prefix: constant.numeric.integer.other.fourcc, constant.numeric.float.real. storage.modifier is qualified per keyword (.constant, .array, .local) so themes can colour them apart - TESH files 'array' with the type keywords, not the modifiers.

Strings are begin/end rules, and a single-quoted literal with no closing quote on its line falls back to one, because these literals only terminate at the closing quote (or end of file), never at a newline.

Constructs that still lex as a single token but are not valid JASS (bad escapes, '$' or '0x' without digits, octal containing 8/9, wrong-length single-quoted literals, a lone '.', a '!' without '=', unrecognized characters) are scoped invalid.illegal.

The globals block ends at 'endglobals' or recovers via lookahead at the next declaration/statement line, so a missing 'endglobals' cannot swallow the rest of the file. The end pattern wins same-offset ties against content patterns.
name: JASS

patterns.comment: The complete set of valid escape characters.
patterns.name: constant.character.escape.jass

patterns.comment: Any other backslash-character pair is consumed as one (invalid) escape.
patterns.name: invalid.illegal.unknown-escape.jass

patterns.comment: A backslash immediately before the end of a line. The newline is not one of the escapable characters, so this is a dangling escape, not a line continuation. The enclosing literal does carry on to the next line, but that is its begin/end rule doing it, not this backslash.
patterns.name: invalid.illegal.unknown-escape.jass

character-literal.comment: Single-quoted literals are measured in UTF-8 BYTES, not characters: exactly 4 bytes between the quotes is a fourCC integer literal ('A000', but also '™a' since '™' is three bytes), exactly 1 byte is a character literal, and any other terminated length is invalid. An escape counts as the byte width of the escaped character. Order matters: fourCC before the wrong-length rule, and the unterminated begin/end fallback last so it only fires when no closing quote exists on the line.

patterns.comment: The alternatives are every ordering of UTF-8 byte widths that sums to 4: 1+1+1+1, 1+1+2, 1+2+1, 2+1+1, 2+2, 1+3, 3+1, 4.
patterns.name: constant.numeric.integer.other.fourcc.jass

patterns.comment: A character literal is a single BYTE, so its content must be ASCII; a multibyte character falls through to the wrong-length rule.
patterns.name: constant.character.jass

patterns.comment: Terminated on the same line but neither 1 nor 4 characters long, including the empty literal ''.
patterns.name: invalid.illegal.character-literal-length.jass

patterns.comment: No closing quote on this line: the literal keeps scanning across lines until one is found.
patterns.name: constant.character.jass

numbers.comment: No boundary anchors on purpose (see invariants). Order: hex before its empty-digits invalid form and before decimal; real before bad-octal so '08.5' is a real; bad-octal before octal so '078' stays one invalid token.

patterns.comment: A lone dot still lexes as a real-literal token, but is not a valid number.
patterns.name: invalid.illegal.number.jass

keywords.comment: Keywords are case-sensitive. The trailing lookahead requires the keyword to end where the identifier-character run ends: it stops 'iffy' from lexing as 'if' + 'fy' and lets 'return' fall through so 'returns' can match. No leading boundary - see invariants.

function-call.comment: Must come after #keywords so 'if (', 'not (' and 'return (' keep their keyword scope.
function-call.name: variable.function.jass

patterns.comment: Two-character operators first: the engine breaks a same-offset tie by rule order, not match length.
patterns.name: keyword.operator.comparison.jass

illegal.comment: Any character no other rule consumed, one at a time - including a lone '!', which is only valid as part of '!='. Only space and tab count as whitespace in JASS, so exotic spaces such as U+000B or U+00A0 are correctly flagged.
illegal.name: invalid.illegal.character.jass

type-slot.comment: A USAGE position the parser treats as a type name. #keywords first, so primitives keep their storage.type.primitive scope and a stray keyword keeps its keyword scope. The fallback is support.type rather than entity.name.type (definitions only): every non-primitive type a script can use is declared by common.j, so a type usage is a library reference. The type-declaration rule scopes its own definition and extends slots separately.

type-declaration.comment: The name slot is the one place a type is DEFINED (entity.name.type); the extends slot names the parent type (entity.other.inherited-class). Both still route through #keywords first, so 'extends handle' keeps handle's primitive scope.
type-declaration.name: meta.declaration.type.jass

global-declaration.comment: Two variants so the name slot can reflect constness (variable.other.constant): a capture's scope cannot depend on another capture, so the 'constant' form is its own rule, listed first to win the same-offset tie. A malformed 'constant NAME' line without a type fails the first variant and degrades through the second, where 'constant' lands in the type slot and keeps its modifier colour via routing.

function-declaration.comment: Covers 'function' and single-line 'native' declarations; the region only spans the signature line, the body is handled by the line-anchored statement rules. The wrapper region itself is unnamed so the meta.function scopes alternate instead of stacking: the begin match (including its trailing whitespace) is the meta.function head, and the takes/returns clauses are sibling regions. The name slot refuses 'takes'/'returns' so a signature missing its name still gets its clause regions.

4.comment: Needs its own meta.function name: a capture tokenized via sub-patterns does not inherit the enclosing capture 1's name.
4.name: meta.function.jass

patterns.comment: A lone identifier in a signature can only be a type.
patterns.name: support.type.jass

function-parameters.comment: The takes-clause, with the 'takes' keyword as its opening delimiter. Ends by lookahead at 'returns', a trailing comment, or end of line, so those all land outside the region. The end lookahead only wins ties at its own offset, which is why #parameter must refuse to consume 'returns' (see there).
function-parameters.name: meta.function.parameters.jass

function-return-type.comment: The returns-clause. Ends by lookahead before a trailing comment or the end of the line.
function-return-type.name: meta.function.return-type.jass

parameter.comment: A 'type name' pair in a parameter list. Both slots try #keywords first, so a keyword landing in either one keeps its keyword scope. The name slot refuses 'returns' because the pair starts left of where the enclosing parameters region's end lookahead fires: without the guard, 'takes nothing returns nothing' would match 'nothing returns' as a pair, consume the keyword, and hold the region open across the return type.

function-reference.comment: 'function Foo' used as a code expression. Line-anchored declarations are listed earlier and win the same-offset tie at the start of a declaration line.
